newsitem.title: USA: Subdued US trade ends with little damage to dollar.
newsitem.headline: Subdued US trade ends with little damage to dollar.

text.p: The dollar regrouped in subdued U.S. trade and ended only slightly weaker versus the mark and yen despite dollar/yen's tumble to a seven-month low in overnight trade amid U.S. and Japan trade tensions.

Overseas news of a 92.7 percent rise in Japan's April current account surplus from a year earlier and comments from U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers urging Japan to avoid rising external surpluses also sent the yen to a 21-month high against a quiet German mark.

"The dollar was poised for a fall overnight and the reiteration by Summers about the current account helped a follow through of what we've seen lately -- people liquidating long dollar/yen positions," said Russell LaScala, chief dealer at Citibank.

"For six out of seven days, dollar/yen has gone lower and from a trading point of view, it looks a little overdone," he said, adding dealers were wary of verbal or actual central bank intervention if the dollar should fall below 110 yen.

The dollar fell to a low of 110.62 yen overseas and closed at 111.27/32 yen, slightly below its U.S. open of 111.40/45. Against the mark, the dollar stayed in a tight range and ended barely lower at 1.7160/65 from 1.7167/72.

The dollar slipped against the mark as uncertainty lingered ahead of a crucial meeting in Amsterdam next Monday and Tuesday regarding the likelihood of Europe meeting its 1999 launch date for a single currency, to be called the euro.
Any delay in the timetable for monetary union would likely benefit the mark, considered a more solid currency than the proposed euro.

Optimistic comments from French, German and other European leaders flooded traders' news screens for a second day but did little to uplift dollar sentiment as dealers dismissed the talk and waited for concrete results.

Weighing the dollar down against the mark this week has been concern a European Union stability pact, which outlines the budgetary requirements for single-currency members, would not be agreed upon at the Amsterdam summit as had previously been expected.
The new French government's demands for job creation measures originally put passage of the pact in doubt, but comments from European leaders on Wednesday suggested compromise could be near.
Muting trade volume was the upcoming release of U.S. retail sales and producer price data for May, scheduled for Thursday and Friday respectively.
"I think overall we've had a lot of concentration on the chance that EMU might get postponed and the trade situation in Japan," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank in New York.
"Over the next few days, I think the market might shift a little bit and concentrate on the U.S. economic data. As for what that means for the dollar, we will have to wait and see," he added.

U.S. asset markets underpinned the dollar ahead of this week's important economic data, with the Dow Jones industrial average gaining over 35 points and the 30-year U.S. Treasury rising 6/32 to yield 6.83 percent in late trade.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.4385/95 from 1.4370/80 and to Canadian $1.3867/72 from C$1.3854/59. The British pound gained to $1.6382/87 from $1.6360/70.
